##  STARTING AND STOPPING PMPROXY  top

    
    
           Normally, **pmproxy** is started automatically at boot time and
           stopped when the system is being brought down.  Under certain
           circumstances it is necessary to start or stop **pmproxy** manually.
           To do this one must become superuser and type
    
           # $PCP_RC_DIR/pmproxy start
    
           to start **pmproxy** , or
    
           # $PCP_RC_DIR/pmproxy stop
    
           to stop **pmproxy**.  Starting **pmproxy** when it is already running is
           the same as stopping it and then starting it again.
    
           Normally **pmproxy** listens for PCP client connections on TCP/IP
           port number 44322 (as well as 44323 with **timeseries** enabled)
           registered at **<https://www.iana.org/> **.  Either the environment
           variable **PMPROXY_PORT** or the **-p** command line option may be used
           to specify alternative port number(s) when **pmproxy** is started; in
           each case, the specification is a comma-separated list of one or
           more numerical port numbers.  Should both methods be used or
           multiple **-p** options appear on the command line, **pmproxy** will
           listen on the union of the set of ports specified via all **-p**
           options and the **PMPROXY_PORT** environment variable.  If non-
           default ports are used with **pmproxy** care should be taken to
           ensure that **PMPROXY_PORT** is also set in the environment of any
           client application that will connect to **pmproxy** , or that the
           extended host specification syntax is used (see [PCPIntro(1)](../man1/PCPIntro.1.html) for
           details).
    

##  DIAGNOSTICS  top

    
    
           If **pmproxy** is already running the message "Error:
           OpenRequestSocket bind: Address already in use" will appear.
           This may also appear if **pmproxy** was shutdown with an outstanding
           request from a client.  In this case, a request socket has been
           left in the TIME_WAIT state and until the system closes it down
           (after some timeout period) it will not be possible to run
           **pmproxy**.
    
           In addition to the standard **PCP** debugging options, see [pmdbg(1)](../man1/pmdbg.1.html),
           **pmproxy** currently supports the debugging option **context** for
           tracing client connections and disconnections.
    

##  FILES  top

    
    
           _$PCP_PMPROXYOPTIONS_PATH_
                command line options for **pmproxy** when launched from
                **$PCP_RC_DIR/pmproxy** All the command line option lines should
                start with a hyphen as the first character.
    
           _$PCP_SYSCONFIG_DIR/pmproxy_
                Environment variables that will be set when **pmproxy**
                executes.  Only settings of the form
                "PMPROXY_VARIABLE=value" will be honoured.

                (or **$PCP_LOG_DIR/pmproxy/pmproxy.log** when started
                automatically)
                All messages and diagnostics are directed here

                default OpenSSL certificate database directory, optionally
                used for Secure Socket Layer connection in **timeseries** mode
                of operation.  These certificates can be created and queried
                using the **openssl** tool, amongst others.

####  3.2.13.1.  Code objects  Â¶

Code objects represent _byte-compiled_ executable Python code, or [ bytecode
](../glossary.html#term-bytecode) . The difference between a code object and a
function object is that the function object contains an explicit reference to
the functionâs globals (the module in which it was defined), while a code
object contains no context; also the default argument values are stored in the
function object, not in the code object (because they represent values
calculated at run-time). Unlike function objects, code objects are immutable
and contain no references (directly or indirectly) to mutable objects.

#  plot.Binomix: Plotting and printing ` Binomix ` objects

##  Description

Generic functions for plotting and printing the content of a ` Binomix `
object.

##  Usage

    
    
    "plot"(x, type="pan", cex=2, ncomp=NA, ...)
    "summary"(object, ...)
    "str"(object, ...)

##  Arguments

x

A ` Binomix ` object, see below.

object

A ` Binomix ` object, see below.

type

Type of plot, default is  type="pan"  which means the pie chart shows
distribution over the entire pan-genome. The alternative is  type="single"
which means the pie chart will show the distribution within a single (average)
genome.

cex

Plot symbol scaling.

ncomp

Which model to display. You can override the display of the optimal (minimum
BIC) model by specifying the number of components here, e.g.  ncomp=5  will
always display the model with  5  components regardless of its BIC value.

...

Optional graphical arguments.

##  Details

A ` Binomix ` object contains a series of fitted binomial mixture models. It
is a small (S3) extension to a ` list ` , having two components. These are
named  BIC.table  and  Mix.list  , see ` [ binomixEstimate
](/link/binomixEstimate?package=micropan&version=1.0) ` for more details. The
` [ plot.Binomix ](/link/plot.Binomix?package=micropan&version=1.0) ` function
will display a ` Binomix ` object as a pie chart. Only the model with the
smallest BIC-criterion value is displayed. The BIC-criterion is used to rank
the various fitted models, and minimum BIC is an objective criterion for
finding the best model complexity. Each sector of the pie chart is a
component, the color of the sector indicates its detection probability and the
size of the sector its mixing proportion. This pie chart illustrates how gene
clusters are distributed within the pan-genome. Sectors of (dark) blue color
are highly conserved gene clusters (core genes), sectors of greenish colors
are medium conserved clusters (shell genes) and sectors of orange/pink colors
are non-conserved clusters (cloud genes). The ` [ summary.Binomix
](/link/summary.Binomix?package=micropan&version=1.0) ` function will print
the estimated core size and pan-genome size for the optimal component model.
The ` [ str.Binomix ](/link/str.Binomix?package=micropan&version=1.0) `
function will simply print the number of models fitted in the ` Binomix `
object.

##  See Also

` [ binomixEstimate ](/link/binomixEstimate?package=micropan&version=1.0) ` .

# How Daylight Saving Time Shifts Influence Global Stock Exchange Hours and Timestamp Accuracy

Twice a year, many parts of the world adjust their clocks to accommodate daylight saving time (DST). While the practice is often discussed in terms of energy savings or social convenience, it has a significant and often underappreciated impact on the functioning of international stock exchanges. The shift affects not only the local opening and closing bells but also the precise timestamps recorded for trades and settlements, with implications for cross-border transactions and market synchronization.

## The Mechanics of DST Adjustments in Exchanges

Stock exchanges operate on tightly defined schedules, often down to the second. When a country observes DST, its local time shifts forward or backward by one hour. Exchanges in these regions must decide whether to alter their published trading hours or maintain them in terms of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

For example, when the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) moves from Eastern Standard Time (EST) to Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), its local trading hours remain 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., but in UTC terms, the schedule shifts. This change can create temporary mismatches with exchanges in regions that do not observe DST or that transition on different dates. The London Stock Exchange, for instance, changes its clocks on a separate schedule from the U.S., which can lead to a period where the overlap in trading hours is shifted by an hour.

## Timestamp Consistency and Cross-Border Settlement

Timestamp accuracy is crucial for regulatory compliance, audit trails, and market integrity. A trade executed at 15:45 local time in Frankfurt during DST might correspond to a different UTC offset than a similar trade executed in Tokyo. If systems are not properly synchronized, discrepancies can occur in recorded times, potentially affecting settlement processes.

Cross-border settlements often rely on matching buy and sell orders across multiple time zones. Any misalignment in timestamps can cause delays or even failed settlements. Financial institutions typically employ time synchronization protocols, sometimes using atomic clock signals, to ensure that all transaction records adhere to a standardized reference—most often UTC.

## Coordination Challenges Across Markets

During the transition periods when some exchanges have shifted to DST and others have not, traders and automated systems must adapt quickly. Algorithmic trading strategies that depend on precise timing may require recalibration. Market data feeds must clearly indicate the time zone of each timestamp to avoid misinterpretation.

For instance, a trader in Hong Kong accessing U.S. market data during the two-week period between the U.S. DST change and Asia’s lack of change must be aware that the time difference is temporarily altered. This can influence decision-making, especially in high-frequency trading where milliseconds matter.

## Operational Responses and Best Practices

Exchanges and financial institutions often publish detailed schedules in advance of DST changes, outlining any temporary shifts in trading overlaps. Some opt to maintain constant UTC trading hours year-round, thereby shifting local times but preserving international consistency. Others adjust their UTC hours to keep local times fixed, accepting the temporary misalignment with foreign markets.

Best practices include:
- **Clear Communication:** Disseminating updated trading hours and settlement cut-off times well before DST transitions.
- **System Synchronization:** Ensuring that all trading, clearing, and settlement systems use the same time reference, ideally UTC.
- **Automated Adjustments:** Implementing software that automatically recalculates time differences and adjusts order execution windows accordingly.

## The Broader Impact on Market Participants

While institutional systems are generally robust against DST-induced timing issues, individual traders and smaller brokerages can be caught off guard. Missing an opening bell by an hour or misinterpreting a timestamp can lead to lost opportunities or errors in reporting.

Moreover, DST changes can subtly impact market liquidity. Altered overlaps between major exchanges may reduce the window for arbitrage opportunities or change the volume profile throughout the trading day. For global investors, understanding these cyclical shifts is part of maintaining an effective trading strategy.

---

Daylight saving time is more than a quirk of the calendar—it is a recurring operational event that reverberates through the complex web of global financial markets. By anticipating the changes in trading hours, ensuring precise timestamp handling, and maintaining clear communication across borders, exchanges and market participants can navigate the twice-yearly shifts without disruption. In a landscape where seconds can mean millions, the clock’s hands are as much a part of market infrastructure as the trading floor itself.

## Introducing the PnP Framework library The PnP Framework library (released as v. 1.0 on January 2021) is the evolution of CSOM and of an old library called PnP Sites Core (now retired and archived). The PnP Framework library targets .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET 5.0/6.0/7.0, so you can use it on any platform (Windows, Linux, MacOS) and in any cloud-based service like Azure App Services, Azure Functions, Containers, etc. By design, this library supports SharePoint Online (SPO) only. If you are developing a modern solution for SharePoint Online using .NET and you would like to have a CSOM-like coding style, you should definitely install the _PnP.Framework_ NuGet package and use it. From a functional point of view, the PnP Framework is a set of extensions built on top of CSOM, it is cross-platform, and it uses the new Client Side Object Model (CSOM) of SPO for .NET Standard. It mainly targets modern authentication with OAuth 2.0, but there is still support for app-only mode in ACS for "already existing" apps. By default, PnP Framework library uses a multi-tenant Azure Active Directory application called _PnP Management Shell_, which you should register in your tenant using the following PnP PowerShell syntax. Copy ```lang-PowerShell Register-PnPManagementShellAccess ``` This will launch a login flow that will ask you to consent to the application. Notice that is only required -once- per tenant. You will need to have appropriate access rights to be able to consent applications in your Azure AD. However, in this article you will rely on modern authentication with a custom AAD application that you have to register and configure for desktop authentication with http://localhost as a supported redirect URI. Important To learn more about using modern authentication and AAD instead of ACS you can read the article Upgrading SharePoint applications from Azure Access Control Service to Azure Active Directory. Now, let's create a .NET console application to consume some SharePoint Online data using the PnP Framework library. First of all, you will need to add a reference to the _PnP.Framework_ nuget package. In Visual Studio you can simply add a package reference using the UI. In Visual Studio Code you will need to execute the following command. Copy ```lang-PowerShell dotnet add package PnP.Framework ``` Once you have done that, your project will reference not only the PnP Framework library, but also the CSOM library, which is internally used by PnP Framework. In the following code sample, you can see how to use the PnP Framework to connect to SPO and consume some data, using an instance of the _AuthenticationManager_ class and the modern authentication with OAuth 2.0. Copy ```lang-CSharp using Microsoft.SharePoint.Client; using PnP.Framework; var clientId = "<client-Id>"; var tenantId = "<tenant-Id>"; var redirectUrl = "<redirect-Url>"; var siteUrl = "<target-Site-Url>"; // Create an instance of the AuthenticationManager type var authManager = AuthenticationManager.CreateWithInteractiveLogin(clientId, redirectUrl, tenantId); // Get a reference to the ClientContext of CSOM using (var context = await authManager.GetContextAsync(siteUrl)) { // Read web properties var web = context.Web; context.Load(web, w => w.Id, w => w.Title); await context.ExecuteQueryRetryAsync(); Console.WriteLine($"{web.Id} - {web.Title}"); // Retrieve a list by title together with selected properties var documents = web.GetListByTitle("Documents", l => l.Id, l => l.Title); Console.WriteLine($"{documents.Id} - {documents.Title}"); // Retrieve the top 10 items from the list var query = CamlQuery.CreateAllItemsQuery(10); var items = documents.GetItems(query); context.Load(items); await context.ExecuteQueryRetryAsync(); // Browse through all the items foreach (var i in items) { Console.WriteLine($"{i.Id} - {i["Title"]}"); } } ``` The above code relies on interactive and web based login to access a target SharePoint Online site. The authentication is managed by the _AuthenticationManager_ class of PnP Framework, which gives you an easy and simplified technique to authenticate against SharePoint Online using any of the following options: - Interactive user authentication - Username and password (where password has to be stored in a _SecureString_) - Device code with an application registered in Azure Active Directory - Authorization Code flow - Client ID and Client Secret for app-only authentication - X.509 Certificate for app-only authentication - On-behalf-of flow - Azure ACS for app-only authentication The code sampleretrieves _Id_ and _Title_ of a library with title "Documents" and it retrieves the top 10 items in the library, in order to show _Id_ and _Title_ of those items. Syntax is really close to what you are used to using in CSOM. In fact, you get a _context_ object, which is of type _Microsoft.SharePoint.Client.ClientContext_ from CSOM, and you use it. However, for example you use the _ExecuteQueryRetryAsync_ method, which is actually a .NET extension method provided by PnP Framework, or you use the _GetListByTitle_ method, which is yet another extension method provided by PnP Framework. Moreover, in PnP Framework there are plenty of asynchronous methods that allow you to write modern asynchronous code. In the PnP Framework library there are thousands of extensions methods for the CSOM types to improve code quality, readability, and efficiency. Furhtermore, in the PnP Framework there is also the implementation of the PnP Provisioning Engine, which is the engine used by many business and by Microsoft itself to automate the provisioning of sites and artifacts. Last but not least, the PnP Framework is in the back-end of most of the cmdlets provided by the PnP PowerShell module, and provides the basic infrastructure for the PnP Page Transformation engine of the PnP Modernization Framework. Generally speaking, the PnP Framework is the "de facto" library that every SharePoint developer should use to create modern solutions for SPO in Microsoft .NET.

#  yield*

The **` yield* ` ** operator is used to delegate to another [ iterable ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Iteration_protocols#the_iterable_protocol)
object, such as a [ ` Generator ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Generator) .

##  Try it

##  Syntax

js

    
    
    yield* expression
    

###  Parameters

` expression ` Optional

    

An iterable object.

###  Return value

Returns the value returned by that iterator when it's closed (when ` done ` is
` true ` ).

##  Description

The ` yield* ` expression iterates over the operand and yields each value
returned by it. It delegates iteration of the current generator to an
underlying iterator â which we will refer to as "generator" and "iterator",
respectively. ` yield* ` first gets the iterator from the operand by calling
the latter's [ ` @@iterator ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Symbol/iterator) method. Then,
each time the ` next() ` method of the generator is called, ` yield* ` calls
the iterator's ` next() ` method, passing the argument received by the
generator's ` next() ` method (always ` undefined ` for the first call), and
yielding the same result object as what's returned from the iterator's `
next() ` method. If the iterator result has ` done: true ` , then the ` yield*
` expression stops executing and returns the ` value ` of that result.

The ` yield* ` operator forwards the current generator's [ ` throw() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Generator/throw) and [ `
return() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Generator/return) methods to
the underlying iterator as well. If the current generator is prematurely
closed through one of these methods, the underlying iterator will be notified.
If the generator's ` throw() ` / ` return() ` method is called, the ` throw()
` / ` return() ` method of the underlying iterator is called with the same
argument. The return value of ` throw() ` / ` return() ` is handled like the `
next() ` method's result, and if the method throws, the exception is
propagated from the ` yield* ` expression.

If the underlying iterator doesn't have a ` throw() ` method, this causes `
yield* ` to throw a [ ` TypeError ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/TypeError) â but before
throwing the error, the underlying iterator's ` return() ` method is called if
one exists. If the underlying iterator doesn't have a ` return() ` method, the
` yield* ` expression turns into a [ ` return ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/return) statement, just like
calling ` return() ` on a suspended [ ` yield ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/yield) expression.

##  Examples

###  Delegating to another generator

In following code, values yielded by ` g1() ` are returned from ` next() `
calls just like those which are yielded by ` g2() ` .

js

    
    
    function* g1() {
      yield 2;
      yield 3;
      yield 4;
    }
    
    function* g2() {
      yield 1;
      yield* g1();
      yield 5;
    }
    
    const gen = g2();
    
    console.log(gen.next()); // {value: 1, done: false}
    console.log(gen.next()); // {value: 2, done: false}
    console.log(gen.next()); // {value: 3, done: false}
    console.log(gen.next()); // {value: 4, done: false}
    console.log(gen.next()); // {value: 5, done: false}
    console.log(gen.next()); // {value: undefined, done: true}
    

###  Other Iterable objects

Besides generator objects, ` yield* ` can also ` yield ` other kinds of
iterables (e.g., arrays, strings, or [ ` arguments ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Functions/arguments) objects).

js

    
    
    function* g3(...args) {
      yield* [1, 2];
      yield* "34";
      yield* args;
    }
    
    const gen = g3(5, 6);

#  BigUint64Array

The **` BigUint64Array ` ** typed array represents an array of 64-bit unsigned
integers in the platform byte order. If control over byte order is needed, use
[ ` DataView ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/DataView)
instead. The contents are initialized to ` 0n ` . Once established, you can
reference elements in the array using the object's methods, or using standard
array index syntax (that is, using bracket notation).

` BigUint64Array ` is a subclass of the hidden [ ` TypedArray ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/TypedArray) class.

##  Constructor

[ ` BigUint64Array() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/BigUint64Array/BigUint64Array)

    

Creates a new ` BigUint64Array ` object.

US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/TypedArray) _ .

[ ` BigUint64Array.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/TypedArray/BYTES_PER_ELEMENT)

    

Returns a number value of the element size. ` 8 ` in the case of `
BigUint64Array ` .

##  Examples

###  Different ways to create a BigUint64Array

js

    
    
    // From a length
    const biguint64 = new BigUint64Array(2);
    biguint64[0] = 42n;
    console.log(biguint64[0]); // 42n
    console.log(biguint64.length); // 2
    console.log(biguint64.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT); // 8
    
    // From an array
    const x = new BigUint64Array([21n, 31n]);
    console.log(x[1]); // 31n
    
    // From another TypedArray
    const y = new BigUint64Array(x);
    console.log(y[0]); // 21n
    
    // From an ArrayBuffer
    const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(64);
    const z = new BigUint64Array(buffer, 8, 4);
    console.log(z.byteOffset); // 8
    
    // From an iterable
    const iterable = (function* () {
      yield* [1n, 2n, 3n];
    })();
    const biguint64FromIterable = new BigUint64Array(iterable);
    console.log(biguint64FromIterable);
    // BigUint64Array [1n, 2n, 3n]

##  Fast scalar value getting and setting  #

Since indexing with ` []  ` must handle a lot of cases (single-label access,
slicing, boolean indexing, etc.), it has a bit of overhead in order to figure
out what youâre asking for. If you only want to access a scalar value, the
fastest way is to use the ` at  ` and ` iat  ` methods, which are implemented
on all of the data structures.

Similarly to ` loc  ` , ` at  ` provides **label** based scalar lookups,
while, ` iat  ` provides **integer** based lookups analogously to ` iloc  `

##  Boolean indexing  #

Another common operation is the use of boolean vectors to filter the data. The operators are: ` |  ` for ` or  ` , ` & ` for ` and  ` , and ` ~  ` for ` not  ` . These **must** be grouped by using parentheses, since by default Python will evaluate an expression such as ` df['A']  > 2  & df['B']  < 3  ` as ` df['A']  > (2  & df['B'])  < 3  ` , while the desired evaluation order is ` (df['A']  > 2)  & (df['B']  < 3)  ` . 

Using a boolean vector to index a Series works exactly as in a NumPy ndarray:

    
    
    In [158]: s = pd.Series(range(-3, 4))
    
    In [159]: s
    Out[159]: 
    0   -3
    1   -2
    2   -1
    3    0
    4    1
    5    2
    6    3
    dtype: int64
    
    In [160]: s[s > 0]
    Out[160]: 
    4    1
    5    2
    6    3
    dtype: int64
    
    In [161]: s[(s < -1) | (s > 0.5)]
    Out[161]: 
    0   -3
    1   -2
    4    1
    5    2
    6    3
    dtype: int64
    
    In [162]: s[~(s < 0)]
    Out[162]: 
    3    0
    4    1
    5    2
    6    3
    dtype: int64
    

You may select rows from a DataFrame using a boolean vector the same length as
the DataFrameâs index (for example, something derived from one of the
columns of the DataFrame):

    
    
    In [163]: df[df['A'] > 0]
    Out[163]:

Find the start and end of a 4-month slice containing a date:

>            TIME_SLICE("DATE", 4, 'MONTH', 'START') AS "START OF SLICE",

>     +------------+----------------+--------------+
>     | DATE       | START OF SLICE | END OF SLICE |
>     |------------+----------------+--------------|
>     | 2019-02-28 | 2019-01-01     | 2019-05-01   |
>     +------------+----------------+--------------+
>  
>

Find the start of 8-hour slices corresponding to two timestamps:
>
>     SELECT '2019-02-28T01:23:45.678'::TIMESTAMP_NTZ AS "TIMESTAMP 1",
>            '2019-02-28T12:34:56.789'::TIMESTAMP_NTZ AS "TIMESTAMP 2",
>            TIME_SLICE("TIMESTAMP 1", 8, 'HOUR') AS "SLICE FOR TIMESTAMP 1",
>            TIME_SLICE("TIMESTAMP 2", 8, 'HOUR') AS "SLICE FOR TIMESTAMP 2";
>
> +-------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------+
>     | TIMESTAMP 1             | TIMESTAMP 2             | SLICE FOR
> TIMESTAMP 1   | SLICE FOR TIMESTAMP 2   |
>
> |-------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------|
>     | 2019-02-28 01:23:45.678 | 2019-02-28 12:34:56.789 | 2019-02-28
> 00:00:00.000 | 2019-02-28 08:00:00.000 |
>

>

Group data into “buckets” based on the date or timestamp (e.g. group data into
buckets that are two weeks wide):
> This example uses the table and data created below:
>  
>  
>     CREATE TABLE accounts (ID INT, billing_date DATE, balance_due NUMBER(11,
> 2));
>  
>     INSERT INTO accounts (ID, billing_date, balance_due) VALUES
>         (1, '2018-07-31', 100.00),
>         (2, '2018-08-01', 200.00),
>         (3, '2018-08-25', 400.00);
>  
>
> Copy
>
> This query shows the bucketed data:
>  
>  
>     SELECT
>            TIME_SLICE(billing_date, 2, 'WEEK', 'START') AS "START OF SLICE",
>            TIME_SLICE(billing_date, 2, 'WEEK', 'END')   AS "END OF SLICE",
>            COUNT(*) AS "NUMBER OF LATE BILLS",
>            SUM(balance_due) AS "SUM OF MONEY OWED"
>         FROM accounts
>         WHERE balance_due > 0    -- bill hasn't yet been paid
>         GROUP BY "START OF SLICE", "END OF SLICE";
>
> +----------------+--------------+----------------------+-------------------+
>     | START OF SLICE | END OF SLICE | NUMBER OF LATE BILLS | SUM OF MONEY
> OWED |
>
> |----------------+--------------+----------------------+-------------------|
>     | 2018-07-23     | 2018-08-06   |                    2 |
> 300.00 |
>     | 2018-08-20     | 2018-09-03   |                    1 |
> 400.00 |
>
> +----------------+--------------+----------------------+-------------------+
>  
>
> Copy
>
> Note that the GROUP BY clause needs both the start of the slice and the end
> of the slice because the compiler expects the GROUP BY clause to contain all
> non-aggregate expressions of the projection clause.

Create a DataFrame:

    
    
    >>> d = {'col1': [1, 2], 'col2': [3, 4]}
    >>> df = pd.DataFrame(data=d)
    >>> df.dtypes
    col1    int64
    col2    int64
    dtype: object
    

Cast all columns to int32:

    
    
    >>> df.astype('int32').dtypes
    col1    int32
    col2    int32
    dtype: object
    

Cast col1 to int32 using a dictionary:

    
    
    >>> df.astype({'col1': 'int32'}).dtypes
    col1    int32
    col2    int64
    dtype: object
    

Create a series:

    
    
    >>> ser = pd.Series([1, 2], dtype='int32')
    >>> ser
    0    1
    1    2
    dtype: int32
    >>> ser.astype('int64')
    0    1
    1    2
    dtype: int64
    

Convert to categorical type:

    
    
    >>> ser.astype('category')
    0    1
    1    2
    dtype: category
    Categories (2, int32): [1, 2]
    

Convert to ordered categorical type with custom ordering:

    
    
    >>> from pandas.api.types import CategoricalDtype
    >>> cat_dtype = CategoricalDtype(
    ...     categories=[2, 1], ordered=True)
    >>> ser.astype(cat_dtype)
    0    1
    1    2
    dtype: category
    Categories (2, int64): [2 < 1]
    

Create a series of dates:

    
    
    >>> ser_date = pd.Series(pd.date_range('20200101', periods=3))
    >>> ser_date
    0   2020-01-01
    1   2020-01-02
    2   2020-01-03
    dtype: datetime64[ns]

##  Name  top

    
    
           pdfmom - produce PDF documents using the _mom_ macro package for
           _groff_
    

##  Synopsis  top

    
    
           **pdfmom**[**-Tpdf**] [_groff-options_] [_file_ ...]
    
           **pdfmom -Tps**[_pdfroff-options_] [_groff-options_] [_file_ ...]
    
           **pdfmom -v**
           **pdfmom --version**
    

##  Description  top

    
    
           _pdfmom_ is a wrapper around _groff_(1) that facilitates the
           production of PDF documents from files formatted with the _mom_
           macros.
    
           _pdfmom_ prints to the standard output, so output must usually be
           redirected to a destination file.  The size of the final PDF can
           be reduced by piping the output through _ps2pdf_(1).
    
           If called with the **-Tpdf** option (which is the default), _pdfmom_
           processes files using _groff_ 's native PDF driver, _gropdf_(1).  If
           **-Tps** is given, processing is passed over to _pdfroff_ , which uses
           _groff_ 's PostScript driver.  In either case, multiple runs of the
           source file are performed in order to satisfy any forward
           references in the document.
    
           _pdfmom_ accepts all the same options as _groff_.  If **-Tps** is given,
           the options associated with _pdfroff_ are accepted as well.  When
           _pdfmom_ calls _pdfroff_ , the options â**-mpdfmark -mom --no-toc** â
           options are implied and should not be given on the command line.
           Equally, it is not necessary to supply the **-mom** or **-m mom** options
           when **-Tps** is absent.
    
           PDF integration with the _mom_ macros is discussed in full in the
           manual âProducing PDFs with _groff_ and _mom_ â, which was itself
           produced with _pdfmom_.
    
           If called with the **-v** or **--version** options, _pdfmom_ displays its
           version information and exits.

# Enhancing Flask Templates with Custom Jinja2 Filters When building dynamic web applications in Flask, templates play a central role in rendering data into HTML. Flask uses the Jinja2 templating engine, which offers a powerful set of features for formatting and transforming data directly within the template layer. One particularly useful capability is the creation of custom filters—small functions that transform data during rendering. This article explores how to register and use custom filters in Jinja2, enabling more expressive and maintainable templates. ## Understanding Jinja2 Filters Filters in Jinja2 are functions applied to variables in the template to modify their output. They are invoked using the pipe syntax (`{{ variable|filter_name }}`), similar to Unix pipelines or functional chaining. Jinja2 comes with a wide set of built-in filters such as `upper`, `lower`, `join`, and `replace`. For example: ```html

{{ username|upper }}

``` This would render the username in uppercase. However, when the built-in set doesn’t meet your needs, custom filters allow you to encode specific transformations unique to your application. ## Creating a Custom Filter in Flask To define a custom filter, you create a Python function and register it with the Flask application’s Jinja2 environment. Here’s a simple example: ```python from flask import Flask app = Flask(__name__) def format_currency(value): return "${:,.2f}".format(value) app.jinja_env.filters['format_currency'] = format_currency ``` In this example, `format_currency` takes a numeric value and returns a formatted currency string. By adding it to `app.jinja_env.filters`, it becomes available in all templates: ```html

Total: {{ total_amount|format_currency }}

``` This separation of logic from presentation keeps templates clean while allowing flexibility in rendering. ## Chaining Filters for Complex Transformations One of the strengths of Jinja2 filters is the ability to chain them. You can apply multiple filters in sequence, with the output of one filter passed as the input to the next: ```html {{ product_name|lower|replace(" ", "_") }} ``` Here the `product_name` is first converted to lowercase, then spaces are replaced with underscores. This chaining allows you to compose transformations without cluttering your Python code. When designing custom filters, it’s important to ensure they operate on predictable input types to avoid unexpected results when chained. ## Filters with Arguments Custom filters can also accept arguments beyond the value they transform. This is useful for parameterizing behavior: ```python def truncate(value, length=50): if len(value) > length: return value[:length] + '...' return value app.jinja_env.filters['truncate'] = truncate ``` You can then call this filter in a template with an argument: ```html

{{ description|truncate(80) }}

``` Arguments allow a single filter to handle multiple variations of a transformation without creating separate functions. ## Organizing Filters for Larger Applications As your application grows, it’s best to organize filters in a dedicated module. This keeps them discoverable and makes maintenance easier: ``` myapp/ filters.py templates/ app.py ``` In `filters.py`, define all your filter functions and a registration function: ```python def register_filters(app): app.jinja_env.filters['format_currency'] = format_currency app.jinja_env.filters['truncate'] = truncate ``` Then in your application setup: ```python from filters import register_filters register_filters(app) ``` This modular approach ensures that templates across the application have access to the same consistent set of filters. ## When to Use Filters vs. View Logic While filters are powerful, they should be used for presentation-oriented transformations rather than core business logic. Heavy computation or data manipulation belongs in the view function or model layer, with filters reserved for formatting, styling, and light transformation. This keeps the template layer focused and maintainable. ## Conclusion Custom Jinja2 filters in Flask provide a clean, declarative way to transform data at render time. By registering well-designed filters, developers can keep templates expressive while avoiding duplication of formatting logic. Whether it’s formatting dates, adjusting text case, or applying custom rules, filters allow for reusable, composable transformations that enhance the clarity and flexibility of your application’s presentation layer. Thoughtful use of this feature can significantly improve the maintainability and readability of complex web projects built with Flask.

    _PCP-PYTHON_(1)            General Commands Manual           _PCP-PYTHON_(1)
    

##  NAME  top

    
    
           **pcp-python** - run a python script using a preferred python variant
    

##  SYNOPSIS  top

    
    
           **pcp python**[_SCRIPT_ [_ARG_] ...]
    

##  DESCRIPTION  top

    
    
           **pcp-python** has been replaced by [pmpython(1)](../man1/pmpython.1.html) which is preferred,
           however **pcp-python** is still installed to provided backwards
           compatibility.
    
           **pcp-python** provides a way to run python scripts using a
           customisable python binary, rather than embedding any particular
           version of python into each script.
    
           This can be useful as it allows version-independent python code
           to be run anywhere.  All python modules shipped with PCP support
           versions 2.6 and later (in the python2 series), and 3.3 and later
           (in the python3 release series).
    
           Due to python monitoring and collecting scripts being relatively
           simple in PCP (not requiring new modules, language features,
           etc), it has been possible to ensure they work for all of the
           above python versions.  Thus, it is common for PCP python scripts
           to use a "shebang" line that invokes **pcp-python** as follows:
    
              _#!/usr/bin/pcp python_
    
           This allows the custom setting to be injected instead of a hard-
           coded python version, while still allowing the user to override
           the python version as follows:
    
              **$ PCP_PYTHON_PROG=python3 /usr/bin/pcp python --version**
              Python 3.3.2
              **$ PCP_PYTHON_PROG=python2 /usr/bin/pcp python --version**
              Python 2.7.5
    
           This is convenient for shipping identical scripts on multiple
           platforms, and for testing different python versions with the one
           script (e.g. in the case where multiple versions of python are
           installed, PCP_PYTHON_PROG can be set in the local environment to
           override the global setting).
    
           By default, the value of PCP_PYTHON_PROG from _/etc/pcp.conf_ will
           be used.  The default value of this configuration parameter is
           set depending on some heuristics about the target build platform.
           These heuristics favour the use of _python3_ in all recent releases
           of PCP, for those platforms that support it.
    

##  PCP ENVIRONMENT  top

    
    
           Environment variables with the prefix **PCP_** are used to
           parameterize the file and directory names used by PCP.  On each
           installation, the file _/etc/pcp.conf_ contains the local values
           for these variables.  The **$PCP_CONF** variable may be used to
           specify an alternative configuration file, as described in
           [pcp.conf(5)](../man5/pcp.conf.5.html).
    

##  SEE ALSO  top

    moment().weekYear(Number);
    moment().weekYear(); // Number
    

Gets or sets the week-year according to the locale.

Because the first day of the first week does not always fall on the first day
of the year, sometimes the week-year will differ from the month year.

For example, in the US, the week that contains Jan 1 is always the first week.
In the US, weeks also start on Sunday. If Jan 1 was a Monday, Dec 31 would
belong to the same week as Jan 1, and thus the same week-year as Jan 1. Dec 30
would have a different week-year than Dec 31.

#  Debugging  ¶

You can connect the debugger in your editor, for example with Visual Studio
Code or PyCharm.

##  Call ` uvicorn ` ¶

In your FastAPI application, import and run ` uvicorn ` directly:

    
    
    import uvicorn
    from fastapi import FastAPI
    
    app = FastAPI()
    
    
    @app.get("/")
    def root():
        a = "a"
        b = "b" + a
        return {"hello world": b}
    
    
    if __name__ == "__main__":
        uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
    

###  About ` __name__ == "__main__" ` ¶

The main purpose of the ` __name__ == "__main__" ` is to have some code that
is executed when your file is called with:

    
    
    $ python myapp.py
    

but is not called when another file imports it, like in:

    
    
    from myapp import app
    

####  More details  ¶

Let's say your file is named ` myapp.py ` .

If you run it with:

    
    
    $ python myapp.py
    

then the internal variable ` __name__ ` in your file, created automatically by
Python, will have as value the string ` "__main__" ` .

So, the section:

    
    
        uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
    

will run.

* * *

This won't happen if you import that module (file).

So, if you have another file ` importer.py ` with:

    
    
    from myapp import app
    
    # Some more code
    

in that case, the automatically created variable inside of ` myapp.py ` will
not have the variable ` __name__ ` with a value of ` "__main__" ` .

So, the line:

    
    
        uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
    

will not be executed.

Info

For more information, check [ the official Python docs
](https://docs.python.org/3/library/__main__.html) .

##  Run your code with your debugger  ¶

Because you are running the Uvicorn server directly from your code, you can
call your Python program (your FastAPI application) directly from the
debugger.

* * *

For example, in Visual Studio Code, you can:

  * Go to the "Debug" panel. 
  * "Add configuration...". 
  * Select "Python" 
  * Run the debugger with the option " ` Python: Current File (Integrated Terminal) ` ". 

It will then start the server with your **FastAPI** code, stop at your
breakpoints, etc.

  * Open the "Run" menu. 
  * Select the option "Debug...". 
  * Then a context menu shows up. 
  * Select the file to debug (in this case, ` main.py ` ). 

It will then start the server with your **FastAPI** code, stop at your

#  RegExp.prototype.unicode

The **` unicode ` ** accessor property of [ ` RegExp ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/RegExp) instances returns
whether or not the ` u ` flag is used with this regular expression.

##  Try it

##  Description

` RegExp.prototype.unicode ` has the value ` true ` if the ` u ` flag was
used; otherwise, ` false ` . The ` u ` flag enables various Unicode-related
features. With the "u" flag:

  * Any [ Unicode code point escapes ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Regular_expressions/Unicode_character_class_escape) ( ` \u{xxxx} ` , ` \p{UnicodePropertyValue} ` ) will be interpreted as such instead of identity escapes. For example ` /\u{61}/u ` matches ` "a" ` , but ` /\u{61}/ ` (without ` u ` flag) matches ` "u".repeat(61) ` , where the ` \u ` is equivalent to a single ` u ` . 
  * Surrogate pairs will be interpreted as whole characters instead of two separate characters. For example, ` /[ð]/u ` would only match ` "ð" ` but not ` "\ud83d" ` . 
  * When [ ` lastIndex ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/RegExp/lastIndex) is automatically advanced (such as when calling [ ` exec() ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/RegExp/exec) ), unicode regexes advance by Unicode code points instead of UTF-16 code units. 

There are other changes to the parsing behavior that prevent possible syntax
mistakes (which are analogous to [ strict mode ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Strict_mode) for regex syntax). These
syntaxes are all [ deprecated and only kept for web compatibility ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Deprecated_and_obsolete_features#regexp) ,
and you should not rely on them.

The set accessor of ` unicode ` is ` undefined ` . You cannot change this
property directly.

###  Unicode-aware mode

When we refer to _Unicode-aware mode_ , we mean the regex has either the ` u `
or the [ ` v ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/RegExp/unicodeSets) flag, in
which case the regex enables Unicode-related features (such as [ Unicode
character class escape ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Regular_expressions/Unicode_character_class_escape)
) and has much stricter syntax rules. Because ` u ` and ` v ` interpret the
same regex in incompatible ways, using both flags results in a [ ` SyntaxError
` ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/SyntaxError) .

# Optimizing Microservices Communication Across Distributed Kubernetes Clusters with Istio

In today’s cloud-native landscape, organizations increasingly deploy microservices across multiple Kubernetes clusters spread across different geographical regions. This multi-cluster setup offers resilience, compliance with data locality laws, and improved latency for regional users. However, it also introduces complexity in service-to-service communication, especially when services must interact seamlessly across cluster boundaries. A powerful solution to this challenge is the use of a service mesh—specifically Istio—to simplify and optimize communication in such distributed environments.

## The Multi-Cluster Communication Challenge

When Kubernetes clusters are deployed in separate datacenters, each cluster maintains its own networking, service discovery, and security contexts. Native Kubernetes services operate well within a single cluster, but cross-cluster communication often requires manual configuration of ingress gateways, DNS resolution, and traffic policies. This complexity can lead to:

- **Inconsistent routing** between services in different clusters.
- **Higher latency** due to inefficient traffic paths.
- **Limited observability** for requests that traverse multiple clusters.
- **Security gaps** in authentication and authorization across boundaries.

Without a unified layer to manage traffic and security, operators often resort to brittle, custom solutions that are difficult to maintain.

## Why Istio?

Istio provides a robust service mesh architecture that abstracts away much of the complexity involved in cross-cluster communication. Its key features—traffic routing, load balancing, observability, and security—are all designed to work across heterogeneous environments.

In a multi-cluster setup, Istio can be configured in two primary modes:

1. **Single control plane, multiple clusters** – One Istio control plane manages the configuration for all clusters, enabling consistent policies and routing rules.
2. **Multiple control planes with mesh federation** – Each cluster runs its own Istio control plane, but they are connected to share service discovery and trust domains.

Both approaches allow services in one cluster to communicate with services in another transparently, using the same Istio-managed mTLS connections and routing logic as they would locally.

## Traffic Routing and Load Balancing Across Regions

Istio’s Envoy proxies intercept traffic between services, applying intelligent routing rules. In a distributed Kubernetes environment, this means requests can be routed based on:

- **Geographic proximity** – Directing users to the closest datacenter for lower latency.
- **Failover policies** – Automatically redirecting traffic to healthy services in other clusters when a local service is unavailable.
- **Traffic splitting** – Gradually shifting load between services in different regions for canary deployments or A/B testing.

For example, a microservice deployed in both a US-East and EU-West cluster can be configured so that European users’ requests are served from EU-West, while US users are served from US-East. If EU-West experiences downtime, Istio can reroute traffic to US-East without manual intervention.

## Observability Across Cluster Boundaries

One of Istio’s strengths is its built-in observability stack, which integrates with tools like Prometheus, Grafana, and Jaeger. In a multi-cluster deployment, this observability extends across all clusters, giving operators a unified view of:

- **Latency metrics** for cross-cluster calls.
- **Error rates** and failure points in inter-cluster communication.
- **Traffic flows** between services, visualized across regions.

This visibility is critical for diagnosing issues that may arise only in cross-cluster scenarios, such as network congestion on inter-datacenter links or misconfigured routing rules.

## Security and Compliance

Security is paramount when services communicate across datacenter boundaries. Istio enforces mTLS (mutual Transport Layer Security) by default, ensuring that all service-to-service traffic is encrypted and authenticated. In multi-cluster meshes, Istio can share a common root of trust, allowing services in different clusters to verify each other’s identities without exposing sensitive credentials.

This approach also aids in compliance with regional data protection laws. By applying Istio’s traffic policies, operators can ensure that certain data never leaves a specific region, while still allowing metadata or authorized requests to traverse clusters.

## Best Practices for Deployment

To make the most of Istio in a distributed Kubernetes environment:

1. **Plan your mesh topology** – Decide between a single control plane or federated control planes based on operational needs and failure domain boundaries.
2. **Use consistent naming conventions** – Ensure service names are unique and resolvable across clusters.
3. **Leverage Istio gateways** – Configure ingress and egress gateways to manage external and inter-cluster traffic securely.
4. **Test failover scenarios** – Simulate cluster outages to verify that routing and load balancing perform as expected.
5. **Monitor continuously** – Use Istio’s observability tools to track performance and adjust policies proactively.

## Conclusion

Deploying microservices across distributed Kubernetes clusters offers significant benefits, but also requires a sophisticated approach to communication, routing, and security. Istio’s service mesh capabilities provide a unified framework for managing these challenges, enabling operators to deliver resilient, performant, and secure services regardless of geographic separation. By embracing Istio’s traffic management, observability, and security features, organizations can unlock the full potential of multi-cluster microservices architectures.

# Designing Scalable Class Hierarchies in Swift: Best Practices for Large Datasets

When building complex applications in Swift, especially those that manage large datasets of custom objects, the design of your class hierarchy can have a significant impact on performance, maintainability, and scalability. By combining thoughtful use of inheritance, protocol-oriented programming, and proper memory management techniques, developers can create systems that are both flexible and efficient.

## Rethinking Inheritance

Inheritance is a powerful tool in Swift, but it can become a liability if overused or misapplied. A scalable hierarchy starts with a clear understanding of the responsibilities of each class. Superclasses should define shared behavior and properties that are truly common across all subclasses, while leaving room for specialized behavior in the subclasses.

For example, a base class might define common attributes for all entities in your application—such as identifiers, creation timestamps, or serialization methods—while subclasses add domain-specific logic. This approach avoids bloating the base class with unrelated functionality and reduces coupling between unrelated parts of the system.

When working with large datasets, minimizing the depth of your inheritance tree can help reduce cognitive load and improve performance, as method dispatch in deep hierarchies can become more complex.

## Embracing Protocol-Oriented Programming

Swift's emphasis on protocol-oriented programming (POP) offers a flexible alternative to deep inheritance chains. Protocols let you define a set of requirements that multiple types can adopt, without forcing them into a rigid class hierarchy. This becomes especially valuable when you have diverse objects that share certain behaviors but differ in their implementation details.

For instance, if multiple object types in your dataset need to be filterable, sortable, or convertible to a display format, you can define protocols for these capabilities. Conforming types implement the requirements in ways that suit their specific contexts, allowing you to create generic algorithms that operate across many types without relying on shared ancestry.

POP also plays well with Swift’s extensions, enabling you to add default implementations to protocols. This reduces code duplication and allows you to evolve your codebase more easily as requirements change.

## Memory Management for Large Collections

Handling large datasets of custom objects requires careful attention to memory usage. In Swift, memory management is handled through Automatic Reference Counting (ARC), but developers still need to be mindful of strong reference cycles and unnecessary retention.

When designing your classes, consider the ownership model for your objects. Use `weak` or `unowned` references for properties that could create cycles, such as parent-child relationships in object graphs. For collections, think about whether you need to store objects strongly or if you can store lightweight representations (like IDs) and fetch the full object only when needed.

If your dataset is truly massive, lazy loading can be an effective strategy. Rather than instantiating all objects at once, you can create them on demand as they are accessed. This reduces initial memory overhead and can improve application startup time.

## Efficient Data Operations

For large datasets, the way you query, filter, and process your objects can significantly affect performance. Leveraging Swift’s higher-order functions (`filter`, `map`, `reduce`, etc.) can make your code more expressive and concise, but be aware of their performance characteristics—particularly when chaining multiple operations.

If you frequently perform operations based on specific properties of your objects, consider indexing or caching results. For example, maintaining a dictionary keyed by a certain property can make lookups instantaneous, avoiding repeated scans through the entire dataset.

## Testing and Evolution

Finally, scalability isn’t just about performance—it’s also about how easily your code can evolve. Well-structured hierarchies and protocol-based designs make it easier to add new object types or modify existing behavior without breaking unrelated parts of the system. Automated tests that validate both individual components and their interactions will help ensure that changes don’t introduce regressions.

As your project grows, periodically review your class hierarchies and protocols to ensure they still reflect the current domain model. Refactoring to simplify relationships and reduce dependencies can keep your codebase healthy over the long term.

---

By combining judicious inheritance, protocol-oriented design, and mindful memory management, Swift developers can build class hierarchies that scale gracefully. The result is a codebase that handles large datasets efficiently while remaining flexible enough to adapt to future needs.

###  Iterative methods

Many array methods take a callback function as an argument. The callback
function is called sequentially and at most once for each element in the
array, and the return value of the callback function is used to determine the
return value of the method. They all share the same signature:

js

    
    
    method(callbackFn, thisArg)

` element `

    

The current element being processed in the array.

` index `

    

The index of the current element being processed in the array.

` array `

    

The array that the method was called upon.

What ` callbackFn ` is expected to return depends on the array method that was
called.

           development branches.
    
           Before a patch is applied, copies of all files the patch modifies
           are saved to the _.pc/_ patch-name directory, where _patch-name_ is
           the name of the patch (for example, _fix-buffer-overflow.patch_).
           The patch is added to the list of currently applied patches
           (_.pc/applied-patches_).  Later, when a patch is regenerated
           (âquilt refreshâ), the backup copies in _.pc/_ patch-name are
           compared with the current versions of the files in the source
           tree using GNU [diff(1)](../man1/diff.1.html).
    
           A similar process occurs when starting a new patch (âquilt newâ);
           the new patch file name is added to the series file.  A file to
           be changed by the patch is backed up and opened for editing
           (âquilt editâ).  After editing, inspect the impact of your
           changes (âquilt diffâ); the changes stay local to your working
           tree until you call âquilt refreshâ to write them to the patch
           file.
    
           Documentation related to a patch can be put at the beginning of
           its patch file (âquilt headerâ).  _Quilt_ is careful to preserve
           all text that precedes the actual patch when doing a refresh.
           (This is limited to patches in unified format; see the GNU
           _Diffutils_ manual.)
    
           The series file is looked up in the _.pc_ directory, in the root of
           the source tree, and in the patches directory.  The first series
           file that is found is used.  This may also be a symbolic link, or
           a file with multiple hard links.  Usually, only one series file
           is used for a set of patches, making the patches subdirectory a
           convenient location.
    
           The _.pc_ directory cannot be relocated, but it can be a symbolic
           link.  Its subdirectories must not be renamed or restructured.
           While patches are applied to the source tree, this directory is
           essential for many operations, including popping patches off the
           stack and refreshing them.  Files in the _.pc_ directory are
           automatically removed when they are no longer needed, so there is
           no need to clean up manually.

# Managed and unmanaged threading in Windows - 03/11/2022 Management of all threads is done through the Thread class, including threads created by the common language runtime and those created outside the runtime that enter the managed environment to execute code. The runtime monitors all the threads in its process that have ever executed code within the managed execution environment. It does not track any other threads. Threads can enter the managed execution environment through COM interop (because the runtime exposes managed objects as COM objects to the unmanaged world), the COM DllGetClassObject function, and platform invoke. When an unmanaged thread enters the runtime through, for example, a COM callable wrapper, the system checks the thread-local store of that thread to look for an internal managed Thread object. If one is found, the runtime is already aware of this thread. If it cannot find one, however, the runtime builds a new Thread object and installs it in the thread-local store of that thread. In managed threading, Thread.GetHashCode is the stable managed thread identification. For the lifetime of your thread, it will not collide with the value from any other thread, regardless of the application domain from which you obtain this value. Section titled: Mapping from Win32 threading to managed threading ## Mapping from Win32 threading to managed threading The following table maps Win32 threading elements to their approximate runtime equivalent. Note that this mapping does not represent identical functionality. For example, **TerminateThread** does not execute **finally** clauses or free up resources, and cannot be prevented. However, Thread.Abort executes all your rollback code, reclaims all the resources, and can be denied using ResetAbort. Be sure to read the documentation closely before making assumptions about functionality. Expand table | In Win32 | In the common language runtime | | --- | --- | | **CreateThread** | Combination of **Thread** and ThreadStart | | **TerminateThread** | Thread.Abort | | **SuspendThread** | Thread.Suspend | | **ResumeThread** | Thread.Resume | | **Sleep** | Thread.Sleep | | **WaitForSingleObject** on the thread handle | Thread.Join | | **ExitThread** | No equivalent | | **GetCurrentThread** | Thread.CurrentThread | | **SetThreadPriority** | Thread.Priority | | No equivalent | Thread.Name | | No equivalent | Thread.IsBackground | | Close to **CoInitializeEx** (OLE32.DLL) | Thread.ApartmentState | Section titled: Managed threads and COM apartments ## Managed threads and COM apartments A managed thread can be marked to indicate that it will host a single-threaded or multithreaded apartment. (For more information on the COM threading architecture, see Processes, Threads, and Apartments.) The GetApartmentState, SetApartmentState, and TrySetApartmentState methods of the Thread class return and assign the apartment state of a thread. If the state has not been set, GetApartmentState returns ApartmentState.Unknown. The property can be set only when the thread is in the ThreadState.Unstarted state; it can be set only once for a thread. If the apartment state is not set before the thread is started, the thread is initialized as a multithreaded apartment (MTA). The finalizer thread and all threads controlled by ThreadPool are MTA. Important For application startup code, the only way to control apartment state is to apply the MTAThreadAttribute or the STAThreadAttribute to the entry point procedure. Managed objects that are exposed to COM behave as if they had aggregated the free-threaded marshaller. In other words, they can be called from any COM apartment in a free-threaded manner. The only managed objects that do not exhibit this free-threaded behavior are those objects that derive from ServicedComponent or StandardOleMarshalObject. In the managed world, there is no support for the SynchronizationAttribute unless you use contexts and context-bound managed instances. If you are using Enterprise Services, then your object must derive from ServicedComponent (which is itself derived from ContextBoundObject). When managed code calls out to COM objects, it always follows COM rules. In other words, it calls through COM apartment proxies and COM+ 1.0 context wrappers as dictated by OLE32. Section titled: Blocking issues ## Blocking issues If a thread makes an unmanaged call into the operating system that has blocked the thread in unmanaged code, the runtime will not take control of it for Thread.Interrupt or Thread.Abort. In the case of Thread.Abort, the runtime marks the thread for **Abort** and takes control of it when it re-enters managed code. It is preferable for you to use managed blocking rather than unmanaged blocking. WaitHandle.WaitOne, WaitHandle.WaitAny, WaitHandle.WaitAll, Monitor.Enter, Monitor.TryEnter, Thread.Join, GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers, and so on are all responsive to Thread.Interrupt and to Thread.Abort. Also, if your thread is in a single-threaded apartment, all these managed blocking operations will correctly pump messages in your apartment while your thread is blocked. Section titled: Threads and fibers ## Threads and fibers The .NET threading model does not support fibers. You should not call into any unmanaged function that is implemented by using fibers. Such calls may result in a crash of the .NET runtime.

**Advancements in Web Scraping for Academic Research: Legal and Ethical Considerations in Automating Data Collection from Government Portals**  

---

**Abstract**  
Recent developments in Python-based web scraping techniques have significantly expanded the capabilities of researchers in the social sciences, economics, and public policy to collect large-scale datasets from publicly accessible government portals. While libraries such as *BeautifulSoup* and *requests* have lowered the technical barrier to entry, the automation of data collection from official sources raises important legal and ethical considerations. This paper examines current technological trends in academic web scraping, evaluates the specific challenges posed by government websites, and outlines best practices for compliance with applicable laws, data protection regulations, and ethical research frameworks.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
Web scraping—the automated extraction of data from websites—has emerged as a valuable tool for academic researchers seeking timely and granular information from public records. Government portals frequently host datasets relevant to taxation, trade, demographics, and regulatory compliance. Using Python libraries such as *BeautifulSoup* and *requests*, researchers can programmatically retrieve, parse, and structure such data for empirical analysis. However, the unique status of government websites as public resources subject to statutory protections necessitates careful consideration of both legal and ethical constraints.

---

**2. Technological Advancements in Python-Based Scraping**  
The Python ecosystem offers a variety of libraries that facilitate HTTP requests, HTML parsing, and data structuring.  

- **Requests Library**: Provides a simplified interface for sending HTTP GET and POST requests, handling cookies, and managing sessions [1].  
- **BeautifulSoup**: Enables the parsing of HTML and XML content into navigable data structures, supporting CSS selectors and tag-based searches [2].  
- **Integration with Data Analysis Tools**: Scraped data can be directly imported into *pandas* DataFrames for cleaning, transformation, and statistical analysis, streamlining the research workflow.  

Recent advancements include asynchronous scraping with *aiohttp* and *asyncio*, which significantly improve efficiency when dealing with large datasets or multiple endpoints. These methods reduce network latency and enable concurrent requests without overloading servers when implemented responsibly.

---

**3. Legal Considerations in Scraping Government Portals**  
Government portals often include terms of service (ToS) or acceptable use policies that govern automated access. Violating these terms may result in legal consequences under computer misuse statutes or contractual law. Key legal considerations include:  

- **Terms of Service Compliance**: Researchers must review and adhere to any explicit restrictions on automated access.  
- **Robots.txt and Technical Barriers**: While not legally binding, the *robots.txt* file signals permissible areas for bot access and should be respected to avoid potential disputes [3].  
- **Data Protection Regulations**: In jurisdictions covered by laws such as the GDPR or Freedom of Information Acts, certain datasets may be subject to privacy protections, requiring anonymization before analysis.  

---

**4. Ethical Frameworks for Automated Data Collection**  
Beyond legality, ethical research practice demands minimizing potential harm and respecting the integrity of public resources. Ethical guidelines include:  

- **Server Load Management**: Implementing rate limiting and backoff strategies to avoid degrading service for other users.  
- **Transparency in Research**: Documenting scraping methodologies, including frequency, scope, and purpose, to ensure reproducibility and accountability.  
- **Respect for Data Integrity**: Avoid altering or misrepresenting scraped content; maintain accurate metadata and timestamps for all collected records.  

Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) increasingly require researchers to outline their web scraping protocols, particularly when accessing sensitive government data that could indirectly identify individuals.

---

**5. Case Studies and Emerging Practices**  
Recent academic projects have successfully employed Python-based scraping to monitor public procurement notices, track environmental compliance reports, and analyze trade flows. In these cases, researchers adhered to official data access APIs where available, or implemented scraping scripts with deliberate delays and caching mechanisms to reduce repeated requests.  

An emerging practice is the hybrid approach: combining scraping with official bulk data downloads to fill gaps in coverage, thereby reducing reliance on continuous automated access. This approach balances the need for up-to-date data with respect for government server resources.

---

**6. Conclusion**  
Advancements in Python web scraping technologies have opened new avenues for academic inquiry into publicly available government datasets. However, the automation of data collection from government portals requires a nuanced understanding of legal frameworks, ethical obligations, and technical best practices. By integrating compliance checks, transparent methodology, and responsible resource usage into their workflows, researchers can leverage these tools while maintaining the integrity of both their work and the public resources they access.

---

**References**  
[1] Reitz, K. (2011). *Requests: HTTP for Humans*. Python Software Foundation.  
[2] Richardson, L. (2004). *BeautifulSoup Documentation*. Crummy.com.  
[3] Koster, M. (1994). *A Standard for Robot Exclusion*. Internet Engineering Task Force Draft.

**Thread Title:** Preserving Hierarchical Folder Structures When Migrating Large XML Batches Between CMS Platforms  

---

**User: data_archiver**  
We’ve been working on a large-scale migration project that involves exporting thousands of XML files from our legacy content management system (CMS) and importing them into a newer platform. The challenge we’re facing is that, during export/import, the original folder hierarchy is getting flattened — all XML files end up in a single directory, losing the organizational structure that was critical to our workflows.  

In the legacy system, XML files were grouped into nested folders by category, project, and date. This made it easy to locate related content and maintain context. After migration, the files are technically intact, but without the directory structure, it’s almost impossible to manage them effectively.  

Has anyone dealt with this kind of path-flattening issue before? How did you ensure the hierarchical relationships between files were preserved during migration?  

---

**User: sys_migrator**  
Yes, I’ve run into this problem when moving data between systems that have different ways of representing file paths. Some CMS platforms store relative paths in metadata fields, while others rely on absolute file system locations. If the export process doesn’t capture these paths correctly, the importer has no way of reconstructing the hierarchy.  

One best practice is to generate a manifest file during export. This manifest should list each XML file along with its full original path. When importing, you can use this manifest to recreate the folder structure in the target system. Even if the CMS doesn’t support deep folder nesting natively, you can simulate it by creating category-based directories and placing files accordingly.  

---

**User: archivist42**  
Another key point: check whether the export tool you’re using compresses the data into a single archive. If so, some tools flatten paths intentionally to avoid conflicts. When that happens, you’ll need to ensure the archive preserves directory paths, such as using TAR or ZIP formats that store relative paths.  

Also, during import, verify that the CMS’s API or batch import tool can accept path information. In our migration, we had to write a pre-processing script that read the manifest and created the folder structure before uploading the XML files. This way, the system received the files in the right structure from the start.  

---

**User: cms_admin**  
In some cases, the problem isn’t with the export but with the way the new CMS indexes content. Certain systems automatically reorganize files into their own internal structure, ignoring the original layout. If that’s the case, you’ll need to look into configuration options that allow “preserve original path” or “import with structure.”  

It’s worth doing a test migration with a small batch first. That lets you confirm whether the hierarchy is being maintained and troubleshoot before moving the full dataset.  

---

**User: data_archiver**  
Thanks for the suggestions! I think the manifest approach might work for us. Our export tool can output a CSV with file paths, so I’ll try using that to rebuild the directory tree before importing. We’ll also check the CMS’s import settings to see if there’s a way to retain the structure automatically.  

---

**User: sys_migrator**  
One last tip: if your XML files contain references to other files (images, linked documents, etc.), make sure those references are updated to match the new folder structure. Even if you preserve the hierarchy, changes in root directory names or relative paths can break links inside the XML. A path-mapping script during migration can prevent this problem.  

---

**Summary:**  
When migrating XML files between CMS platforms, preserving hierarchical folder structures requires careful planning. Export tools must capture original paths, and import processes should reconstruct or simulate the hierarchy. Using a manifest file, choosing archive formats that store relative paths, and validating CMS configuration settings are effective strategies to avoid path flattening. Small-scale test runs and path-mapping scripts can help ensure that both the structure and internal references remain intact post-migration.

# Building a Dynamic Weather Dashboard with JavaScript and Real-Time APIs Creating an engaging and informative weather dashboard is a great way to combine JavaScript skills with data visualization techniques. By connecting to meteorological APIs, you can present users with up-to-the-minute conditions and interactive charts for temperature, humidity, and wind speed. In this tutorial, we’ll walk through the process step-by-step, from fetching the data to rendering it in an appealing, dynamic interface. --- ## 1. Setting Up the Project Structure Begin with a clean HTML and CSS scaffold for your dashboard. Your HTML should contain sections for current conditions, forecast charts, and any additional widgets such as location selection or unit toggles. Example HTML snippet: ```html

Current Weather

``` The CSS can style these sections for clarity and responsiveness, ensuring the dashboard looks good on both desktop and mobile devices. --- ## 2. Choosing a Weather API Select a reliable API that offers real-time meteorological data. Popular choices include: - **OpenWeatherMap** (requires a free API key) - **WeatherAPI** - **Meteorological agency APIs** for your region These APIs generally return JSON objects containing temperature, humidity, wind speed, and other parameters. --- ## 3. Fetching Data with JavaScript Use the `fetch` API to retrieve weather data. Here’s a basic example using OpenWeatherMap: ```javascript async function getWeatherData(city) { const apiKey = 'YOUR_API_KEY'; const url = `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=${city}&units=metric&appid=${apiKey}`; const response = await fetch(url); const data = await response.json(); return { temperature: data.main.temp, humidity: data.main.humidity, windSpeed: data.wind.speed, description: data.weather[0].description }; } ``` This function returns a simplified object containing the key metrics we’ll display. --- ## 4. Rendering Current Conditions Once you have the data, update your DOM elements dynamically: ```javascript function renderCurrentWeather(weather) { const summary = document.getElementById('weather-summary'); summary.innerHTML = `

Temperature: ${weather.temperature}°C

Humidity: ${weather.humidity}%

Wind Speed: ${weather.windSpeed} m/s

Conditions: ${weather.description}

`; } ``` By calling `renderCurrentWeather()` after fetching data, you keep the display in sync with the latest information. --- ## 5. Creating Interactive Charts For visualizing trends, integrate a charting library such as **Chart.js**. This allows you to plot temperature, humidity, and wind speed over time. Example temperature chart setup: ```javascript const ctxTemp = document.getElementById('temperatureChart').getContext('2d'); const temperatureChart = new Chart(ctxTemp, { type: 'line', data: { labels: [], // timestamps will go here datasets: [{ label: 'Temperature (°C)', data: [], borderColor: 'rgba(255, 99, 132, 1)', fill: false }] }, options: { responsive: true, scales: { x: { title: { display: true, text: 'Time' } }, y: { title: { display: true, text: 'Temperature (°C)' } } } } }); ``` You can update the chart’s `labels` and `data` arrays with new points as you fetch fresh readings. --- ## 6. Automating Updates To keep the dashboard current, set up periodic data retrieval using `setInterval`: ```javascript setInterval(async () => { const weather = await getWeatherData('Rome'); renderCurrentWeather(weather); // Update chart datasets here }, 60000); // refresh every minute ``` This approach ensures your users always see the latest conditions without manual refresh. --- ## 7. Enhancing User Interaction Consider adding features such as: - **City search**: Allow users to input a location and fetch its weather data. - **Unit toggles**: Switch between metric and imperial units. - **Forecast charts**: Extend data visualization to multi-day forecasts. These enhancements make the dashboard more versatile and engaging. --- ## Conclusion By combining JavaScript’s data fetching capabilities with a charting library, you can create a weather dashboard that’s both informative and visually appealing. The key steps involve selecting a robust weather API, structuring your interface for clarity, dynamically updating DOM elements, and rendering interactive charts for core metrics. With periodic updates and user-friendly features, your dashboard can provide a real-time window into meteorological conditions anywhere in the world.

The modified class is reported below; the problem was that Pydantic understands (for a timedelta field) int and floats as seconds (source). ```hljs python class MillisecondTimedelta(timedelta): @classmethod def __get_validators__(cls): yield cls.validate @classmethod def validate(cls, v): if any(isinstance(v, t) for t in (int, float)): return cls(milliseconds=v) ``` Now everything should work correctly. ```hljs python >>> data = {"td": 1000} >>> print(MyModel(**data)) td=MillisecondTimedelta(seconds=1) ``` EDIT: Without a custom class and a validator, it's possible to use a function to edit the value to assign to the class constructor; it's required to decorate this function, as seen here ```hljs python class MyModel(BaseModel): td: timedelta @validator('td') def convert_to_ms(cls, v): return v / 1000 ``` Also this solution is working: ```hljs python >>> data = {"td": 3000} >>> print(MyModel(**data)) td=datetime.timedelta(seconds=3) ``` Share Share a link to this answer Copy link CC BY-SA 4.0 Improve this answer Follow Follow this answer to receive notifications edited Feb 7, 2021 at 12:36 answered Feb 7, 2021 at 12:09 !crissal's user avatar crissal crissal 2,6571010 silver badges2727 bronze badges 5 - Aha, so you're instantiating a `timedelta` in the validator and returning that.
